passages.p1:
Eight friends A, B, C, D, E, F, G and H sit around a circular table, all facing the centre. For any person, 'immediate left' is the next seat clockwise and 'immediate right' is the next seat anticlockwise.
H sits opposite A. D sits immediate left of A. B sits third to the left of A. F sits between D and B. C sits immediate left of H. G sits immediate right of A.
passages.p2:
Six lectures P, Q, R, S, T and U are scheduled on six consecutive days from Monday to Saturday, one lecture per day.
P is scheduled on the day immediately before U. R is scheduled before P, with exactly one lecture between R and P. Q is scheduled after U. T is scheduled before R.
passages.p3:
Six friends P, Q, R, S, T and U have different heights.
R is taller than P but shorter than Q. S is taller than only U. T is taller than R but shorter than Q.

questions.text:
Select the option that is related to the third number in the same way as the second number is related to the first.

8 : 65 :: 5 : ?
steps: Apply the same rule: 5² = 25
questions.trap: Taking the square and forgetting the + 1.
wrongReasons: Used n² − 1 instead of n² + 1
Used n × (n + 1)
Stopped at n²
questions.shortcut: 65 is one more than 64, a perfect square: test n² + 1 first.

questions.text: Select the odd one out.
questions.explanation: Kolkata, Mumbai and Chennai are all port cities on a coast or tidal river. Hyderabad is an inland city with no seaport.
steps: Check what the three cities share: they are ports
Hyderabad is inland
So it is the odd one
questions.trap: Looking for a language or state link instead of the port link.
wrongReasons: A major seaport on the Hooghly river
A major seaport on the Arabian Sea
A major seaport on the Bay of Bengal
questions.approach: Look for a geographic or functional link shared by exactly three items.

questions.text: Select the number-triplet that is different from the other three.
questions.explanation: In the other triplets each number is 9 more than the previous one. In (14, 25, 35) the gaps are 11 and 10.
steps: 14, 25, 35: gaps 11, 10, so this is the odd one
questions.trap: Comparing totals instead of the gaps.
wrongReasons: Common difference of 9
Common difference of 9
Common difference of 9
questions.shortcut: Check the two gaps in each triplet; three will match.

questions.text:
What should come in place of the question mark?

12, 14, 18, 26, 42, ?
questions.explanation: The differences double each time: 2, 4, 8, 16, so the next difference is 32. 42 + 32 = 74.
steps: Next difference = 32
questions.trap: Repeating the last difference (16) instead of doubling it.
wrongReasons: Added 16 to 42
Added 24 to 42
Doubled 42
questions.shortcut: Subtract 2 from each term: 10, 12, 16, 24, 40 shows a doubling pattern 2, 4, 8, 16.

Option A (Figure A) is out: This is the left-right mirror image.
Option B (Figure B) is out: This is a rotation.
Option D (Figure D) is out: This is both flips, i.e. a 180° rotation.
Common slip to avoid: Choosing the left-right inversion.
So the answer is option C: Figure C.
questions.trap: Choosing the left-right inversion.

This is a rotation

questions.text: In a certain code language, ROUTES is written as SNWRHP. How will PLANET be written in that code?
questions.explanation: ROUTES → SNWRHP uses the shifts +1, −1, +2, −2, +3, −3. Apply them to PLANET: P+1=Q, L−1=K, A+2=C, N−2=L, E+3=H, T−3=Q.
steps: Apply to PLANET
Code: QKCLHQ
questions.trap: Missing that the shift sizes grow while the direction alternates.
wrongReasons: Last letter shifted −4 instead of −3
Second letter shifted +1 instead of −1
Third letter shifted +3 instead of +2
questions.shortcut: Work out only the first two or three shifts, then test the rule on the remaining letters.

questions.text: In a certain code, every vowel in a word is replaced by the letter immediately before it in the alphabet, and every consonant is replaced by the letter immediately after it. How will EDUCATION be written in that code?
questions.explanation: Vowels (E, U, A, I, O) move one letter back: D, T, Z, H, N. Consonants (D, C, T, N) move one letter forward: E, D, U, O. Reading EDUCATION letter by letter gives D E T D Z U H N O.
steps: E (vowel) → D
D (consonant) → E
U (vowel) → T
C (consonant) → D
A (vowel) → Z
T (consonant) → U
I (vowel) → H
O (vowel) → N
N (consonant) → O
questions.trap: Applying one rule to every letter, or forgetting that A goes back to Z.
wrongReasons: A replaced by B instead of Z
E replaced by F instead of D
C replaced by E instead of D
questions.shortcut: Mark each letter V or C first; then apply the correct shift to each.

questions.explanation: Each fold reflects the hole across the fold line, so one punch gives four holes, one in each quarter, placed symmetrically about both centre lines.
steps: Spot what the question tests: Fold line = mirror line for punched holes.
Option A (Figure A) is out: Only two holes: it misses the second fold.
Option B (Figure B) is out: Only two holes on a diagonal, which ignores one fold.
Option C (Figure C) is out: Has a stray hole at the centre and a missing quarter.
Common slip to avoid: Forgetting that two folds give four holes, or placing the extra holes diagonally only.
So the answer is option D: Figure D.
questions.trap: Forgetting that two folds give four holes, or placing the extra holes diagonally only.
questions.revise: Fold line = mirror line for punched holes

Only two holes on a diagonal, which ignores one fold

questions.text: A is the sister of B. C is the mother of B. D is the father of C. E is the mother of D. How is E related to A?
questions.explanation: C is the mother of A and B. D is C's father, so D is A's grandfather. E is D's mother, so E is A's great-grandmother.
steps: A and B are siblings; C is their mother
D is C's father: A's grandfather
E is D's mother: A's great-grandmother
questions.trap: Stopping one generation short and answering 'grandmother'.
wrongReasons: That would be C's mother, not C's father's mother
E is two generations above C, not a sibling of a parent
No marriage link is given between A and E
questions.shortcut: Count generations upward: mother (1), her father (2), his mother (3) = great-grandmother.

questions.text: A is the father of B and C. C is the husband of D. D is the daughter of E. F is the only son of E. How is F related to C?
questions.explanation: D is C's wife. F is the only son of E, so he is D's brother. A wife's brother is the husband's brother-in-law.
steps: C is married to D
D and F are children of E, so F is D's brother
F is the brother of C's wife: brother-in-law
questions.trap: Calling F a brother because the names share a family.
wrongReasons: F is not a sibling of C's parent
F is the brother of C's wife, not of C
E, not F, is C's father-in-law
questions.approach: Link each person to the person they are married to or descended from, then name the relation.

questions.text: Meena starts from point P and walks 15 m towards the west. She turns left and walks 12 m, turns left again and walks 15 m, and then turns right and walks 9 m. How far and in which direction is she from P?
questions.explanation: West 15 m takes her to (−15, 0). Left from west is south: 12 m to (−15, −12). Left from south is east: 15 m to (0, −12). Right from east is south: 9 m to (0, −21). She is 21 m south of P.
steps: Left → south 12: (−15, −12)
Left → east 15: (0, −12)
Right → south 9: (0, −21)
Distance 21 m, due south
questions.trap: Adding the 15 m legs together instead of seeing that they cancel.
questions.revise: Left and right turns relative to the facing direction
wrongReasons: Subtracted 12 − 9 instead of adding
Added the two 15 m legs instead of cancelling them
Ignored the final 9 m leg
questions.shortcut: The two 15 m legs are in opposite directions and cancel; only 12 + 9 = 21 m south remains.

questions.explanation: All parrots are birds, so P lies inside B. Some pets are birds and some may be parrots, so T overlaps both B and P.
steps: Spot what the question tests: Venn: subset, overlap, disjoint.
Option B (Figure B) is out: Parrots sits outside birds, which is false.
Option C (Figure C) is out: Parrots and pets are swapped.
Option D (Figure D) is out: Birds, parrots and pets are drawn as separate sets.
Common slip to avoid: Drawing pets as separate from parrots.
So the answer is option A: Figure A.
questions.trap: Drawing pets as separate from parrots.
wrongReasons: Parrots sits outside birds, which is false
Parrots and pets are swapped
Birds, parrots and pets are drawn as separate sets

questions.text: In a class of 60 students, Ravi ranks 17th from the top and Amit ranks 22nd from the bottom. How many students are there between Ravi and Amit?
questions.explanation: Amit's rank from the top is 60 − 22 + 1 = 39. Students between rank 17 and rank 39 = 39 − 17 − 1 = 21.
steps: Amit from top = 60 − 22 + 1 = 39
Between = 39 − 17 − 1
questions.trap: Subtracting 17 from 39 and forgetting to drop one place.
questions.revise: Rank from top and bottom, persons between
wrongReasons: Forgot to remove Ravi's own place
Used Amit's rank from the bottom directly
Added 1 twice
questions.shortcut: Persons between = difference of the two ranks (same end) − 1.

questions.text:
Statements:
Only a few cars are buses.
All buses are trains.
No train is a bike.

Conclusions:
I. Some cars are trains.
II. No bike is a bus.
III. Some cars are bikes.

Which of the conclusions follow(s)?
options: All I, II and III follow
questions.explanation: Some cars are buses and all buses are trains, so some cars are trains (I). No train is a bike, so no bus is a bike (II). Cars and bikes are not linked, so III is uncertain.
steps: Some cars are buses, and all buses are trains: some cars are trains (I)
Buses ⊂ trains, and trains share nothing with bikes: no bike is a bus (II)
Nothing links cars to bikes definitely: III fails
questions.trap: Treating 'some cars are not buses' as proof that those cars are bikes.
questions.revise: 'Only a few' statements: some are, some are not
wrongReasons: II also follows: buses are trains and no train is a bike
III is only a possibility, since some cars are not buses
III does not follow
questions.approach: Translate 'only a few A are B' into 'some A are B' and 'some A are not B' before drawing.

questions.text: Which of the following best describes the relationship among Mothers, Women and Doctors?
options: Mothers form a part of Women; Doctors overlaps both Women and Mothers
The three groups are completely separate
Women form a part of Doctors; Mothers is separate
Doctors form a part of Mothers, and both lie inside Women
questions.explanation: Every mother is a woman, so Mothers lies inside Women. Doctors include women and men, and some mothers can be doctors, so Doctors overlaps both Women and Mothers but is not contained in either.
steps: Mothers ⊂ Women
Doctors include men, so Doctors is not inside Women
Some women and some mothers are doctors: overlap with both
questions.trap: Placing Doctors fully inside Women.
questions.revise: Venn relations among three common groups
wrongReasons: Some mothers and women are doctors
Not all women are doctors, and mothers are women
Not all doctors are mothers, and men can be doctors
questions.shortcut: Subset first, then find which group crosses the boundary.

questions.text: Who sits second to the right of D?
questions.explanation: Going clockwise from A: A, D, F, B, H, C, E, G. For D, immediate right is the next seat anticlockwise (A) and the second to the right is G.
steps: H opposite A; D immediate left of A; B third left of A
F between D and B; C immediate left of H
G immediate right of A; E takes the last seat
Clockwise: A, D, F, B, H, C, E, G
Right of D: A (first), G (second)
questions.trap: Counting to the left (clockwise) instead of to the right.
questions.revise: Left and right in circular seating facing the centre
wrongReasons: H sits second to the left of C, not second to the right of D
E sits between C and G
C sits immediate left of H

questions.text: Which lecture is scheduled on Thursday?
questions.explanation: P is immediately before U. R is two days before P, and T is before R. With U on Friday and Q after U on Saturday, P is on Thursday, R on Tuesday, T on Monday and S on Wednesday.
steps: R is two days before P, and T is before R
So R can only be Tuesday (P Thursday) when T takes Monday
U is the day after P: Friday; Q after U: Saturday
S takes the remaining day, Wednesday
Mon T, Tue R, Wed S, Thu P, Fri U, Sat Q
questions.trap: Placing P earlier because R and P are only two days apart.
wrongReasons: U is on Friday
S is on Wednesday

questions.text: A grid of 4 rows and 5 columns is shown. How many squares of all sizes does it contain?

steps: Spot what the question tests: Squares in an m x n grid = sum of (m-k+1)(n-k+1).
Option A (20) is out: Only 1x1 squares counted.
Option C (38) is out: 4x4 squares forgotten.
Option D (60) is out: Rectangles counted along with squares.
Common slip to avoid: Counting only the 12 small squares or forgetting the 3x3 squares.
So the answer is option B: 40.
questions.trap: Counting only the 12 small squares or forgetting the 3x3 squares.
questions.revise: Squares in an m x n grid = sum of (m-k+1)(n-k+1)

4x4 squares forgotten
Rectangles counted along with squares

questions.text: Who is the third tallest among the six friends?
questions.explanation: S is taller than only U, so S is fifth and U is sixth. The remaining four are ordered Q > T > R > P. The order is Q, T, R, P, S, U, so R is third.
steps: S is fifth and U is sixth
T is between Q and R: Q > T > R
P is shorter than R: R > P
Order: Q, T, R, P, S, U
Third tallest = R
questions.trap: Putting P above R after reading 'R is taller than P' backwards.
wrongReasons: T is second tallest
P is fourth tallest
Q is the tallest

questions.text: How many triangles are there in the following figure?
questions.explanation: Seven lines meet at the apex, so any two of them with the base form a triangle: C(7,2) = 21.
steps: Spot what the question tests: Triangles = C(k,2) for k lines from the apex.
Option A (6) is out: Only the smallest triangles counted.
Option B (15) is out: One line fewer assumed.
Option C (28) is out: One extra line assumed.
Common slip to avoid: Counting only the 5 small triangles.
So the answer is option D: 21.

questions.text: Two positions of the same cube are shown. Which number is on the face opposite to 3?
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 260 125" role="img"><polygon points="70,20 115,40 70,60 25,40" stroke="#222" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><polygon points="25,40 70,60 70,110 25,90" stroke="#222" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><polygon points="70,60 115,40 115,90 70,110" stroke="#222" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><text x="66" y="45" font-size="15">5</text><text x="40" y="82" font-size="15">1</text><text x="86" y="82" font-size="15">3</text><polygon points="190,20 235,40 190,60 145,40" stroke="#222" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><polygon points="145,40 190,60 190,110 145,90" stroke="#222" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><polygon points="190,60 235,40 235,90 190,110" stroke="#222" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><text x="186" y="45" font-size="15">5</text><text x="160" y="82" font-size="15">2</text><text x="206" y="82" font-size="15">1</text></svg>
questions.explanation: Between the two views the cube is turned about the vertical axis with 5 on top. Face 3 has turned out of view and the face now at the left (2) came from behind it, so 2 is opposite 3.
steps: Spot what the question tests: Dice: a face never appears together with its opposite.
Option A (1) is out: 1 is adjacent to 3 in the first view.
Option B (5) is out: 5 is adjacent to 3: both are visible together.
Option C (4) is out: 4 is never visible, so it cannot be fixed by these views.
Common slip to avoid: Choosing 1, which is next to 3 in the first view.
So the answer is option D: 2.
questions.trap: Choosing 1, which is next to 3 in the first view.
questions.revise: Dice: a face never appears together with its opposite
wrongReasons: 1 is adjacent to 3 in the first view
5 is adjacent to 3: both are visible together
4 is never visible, so it cannot be fixed by these views

questions.text:
Find the missing number.

(4, 6, 20), (5, 7, 30), (6, 8, ?)
questions.explanation: In each triplet the third number is the first × (second − 1): 4 × 5 = 20 and 5 × 6 = 30. So 6 × 7 = 42.
questions.trap: Using the product of the first two numbers only.
wrongReasons: Used 6 × 8 − 8
Used 6 × 8 without subtracting
Used 6 × 8 − 4

questions.text:
Find the missing number.

Row 1: 7, 3, 16
Row 2: 9, 4, 25
Row 3: 11, 5, ?
questions.explanation: In every row the third number is the first number plus the square of the second: 7 + 3² = 16 and 9 + 4² = 25. So 11 + 5² = 36.
questions.trap: Trying products of the first two numbers, which do not fit.

questions.text:
In the following question, the symbols have their usual meanings. Statements: M < N ≤ O = P ≤ Q > R, with P > R given as a separate statement.

Conclusions:
I. M < P
II. Q > N
III. R < O

Which of the conclusions definitely follow(s)?
options: All I, II and III follow
questions.explanation: M < N ≤ O = P gives M < P (I). P > R and O = P gives R < O (III). From N ≤ O = P ≤ Q we only get Q ≥ N, so Q > N (II) is not certain.
steps: M < N and N ≤ O = P, so M < P: I follows
P > R and O = P, so O > R: III follows
N ≤ O = P ≤ Q gives Q ≥ N only, so II fails
questions.trap: Reading a chain of ≤ signs as a strict inequality.
wrongReasons: II is not certain because Q ≥ N only
I also follows: M < N ≤ O = P
II does not definitely follow
questions.shortcut: One '≤' anywhere in the chain turns a '>' conclusion into a 'maybe'.

steps: Use |30H − 5.5M| with H = 7, M = 40

questions.text:
Who is the youngest among P, Q, R and S?

I. R is younger than P and S.
II. Q is older than R but younger than S.
options: Both statements together are sufficient, but neither alone is
Neither statement is sufficient even together
questions.explanation: Statement I gives R < P and R < S but says nothing about Q, so Q or R could be youngest. Statement II gives R < Q < S but says nothing about P. Together, R is younger than P, S and Q, so R is the youngest.
steps: I alone: R < P, R < S, Q unknown: not enough
II alone: R < Q < S, P unknown: not enough
Together: R < P, R < Q, R < S
R is the youngest
questions.trap: Stopping after one statement because it seems to point to R.
wrongReasons: Q could still be younger than R
P could still be younger than R
Together they make R younger than P, Q and S
questions.approach: Test each statement separately, looking for a second possible answer, then combine.

questions.text:
Statement: 'The company has announced a 20% discount on all its products for one week to attract more customers.'

Assumptions:
I. A discount can attract more customers.
II. Customers are unaware of the company's products.

Which of the assumptions is/are implicit in the statement?
options: Both I and II are implicit
Neither I nor II is implicit
questions.explanation: The company announces a discount in order to attract customers, so it must believe discounts attract customers (I). Nothing in the statement suggests that customers do not know the products (II).
steps: Ask what the company must believe for the plan to be sensible
It believes discounts attract customers: I is implicit
No need to assume customers are unaware: II is not implicit
questions.trap: Picking an assumption that merely sounds possible.
questions.revise: Statement and assumption: what must be true for the plan to make sense
wrongReasons: The aim is more customers, not awareness of products
II is not needed for the plan to make sense
I is the very belief behind the announcement
questions.shortcut: An assumption is implicit only if the statement would be pointless without it.
